questions.stem: You are examining Bob, 20, in ED after a fall onto his left side while mountain biking. He is sitting up and breathless, BP 88/60, HR 134, and his neck veins are distended. Which examination step best tells a tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade at the bedside?
options: Listen for muffled heart sounds over the praecordium
Check for a pulsus paradoxus with the BP cuff
Percuss and auscultate both hemithoraces, comparing left with right
Assess the jugular venous pressure with him reclined at 45 degrees
questions.why: Distended neck veins with hypotension after chest trauma can mean tension or tamponade. One-sided hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds, plus tracheal deviation, points to tension. In tamponade the chest is resonant and breath sounds are equal on both sides.
notes: Heart sounds are hard to judge in a noisy resus bay, and muffling is an unreliable sign that does not localise anything to one hemithorax.
Pulsus paradoxus can occur in both tamponade and tension pneumothorax, and it takes too long to measure in a shocked patient.
The JVP is raised in both conditions so it does not separate them, and Bob is worse lying flat.

questions.stem: Bob, 20, has a left tension pneumothorax after a bike fall. Needle decompression at the left 4th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line, releases a rush of air. On high-flow oxygen his BP comes up to 112/70 and SpO2 to 96%. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the chest X-ray in 4 hours and remove the cannula if the lung is up
Insert a left intercostal catheter in the safe triangle on an underwater seal
Aspirate through the cannula and discharge him if the lung re-expands
Arrange a CT chest to define the air leak before any further intervention
questions.why: Needle decompression only buys time. The cannula can kink, dislodge or block, and tension can come back. A traumatic tension pneumothorax needs a definitive intercostal catheter in the 4th or 5th space in the safe triangle, attached to an underwater seal drain.
notes: Leaving only a cannula risks the tension coming back, and a traumatic pneumothorax that has already caused tension needs a drain, not watchful waiting.
Aspiration and discharge are for selected primary spontaneous pneumothoraces, not a traumatic tension pneumothorax with shock.
CT does not replace treatment. Definitive drainage should not be delayed for imaging in a patient who has just come out of obstructive shock.

questions.stem: Bob, 20, fell onto his left side mountain biking. Within an hour he has a BP of 88/60, HR 134, distended neck veins and a trachea deviated to the right. His Hb is 148. What is the main mechanism of his hypotension?
options: Blood loss into the left pleural space reducing circulating volume
Hypoxic depression of left ventricular contractility
Loss of sympathetic tone causing widespread vasodilation
Raised intrathoracic pressure compressing the venae cavae, cutting venous return
questions.why: A one-way valve traps air in the pleural space with each breath, and intrathoracic pressure rises. The mediastinum shifts, the venae cavae are compressed and kinked, and preload falls, so cardiac output drops. This is obstructive shock, which is why the neck veins are distended.
notes: Haemorrhagic shock gives flat neck veins and a dull hemithorax, and his chest is hyper-resonant with no effusion on the X-ray.
His hypoxia is moderate (SpO2 91%). The main problem is a lack of venous filling, not a failing pump.
Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury and causes bradycardia with warm peripheries. Bob is tachycardic, with no neck injury or neurological deficit.

questions.stem: During Bob's left chest decompression, the registrar advances the needle just over the upper border of the 5th rib, anterior to the mid-axillary line. This technique avoids the main intercostal neurovascular bundle. Where does that bundle lie?
options: Lower border of the rib above, between internal and innermost intercostals
Upper border of the rib below, between external and internal intercostals
Lower border of the rib above, superficial to the external intercostal
Midway across the space, just deep to the parietal pleura
questions.why: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve (VAN, top to bottom) run in the costal groove along the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Going in just over the top of the rib below keeps the needle or drain away from them.
notes: Going over the upper border of the rib below is the safe route. The main bundle is not there, and it lies deep to the internal intercostal, not between the external and internal.
The bundle is in the costal groove, but it lies deep to both the external and internal intercostals, not superficial to them.
The bundle runs in the costal groove of the rib above, not across the middle of the space, and it lies outside the endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura.
